title: Scottish democratic legitimacy combines durable voting norms with low perceived influence, weakened institutional trust, and economic insecurity gradients
source_unit: Scottish Government, Scottish Social Attitudes Survey 2025: Core Module
geography: Scotland; nationally representative survey of adults aged 16 and over

observations.period: September-November 2025 fieldwork; published June 2026 and corrected September 2026; social trust

denominator.unit: completed Scottish Social Attitudes Survey core-module surveys; weighted estimates

most_people_trusted.unit: percent saying most people can be trusted

cant_be_too_careful.unit: percent saying they cannot be too careful dealing with people

low_income_trust_gradient.value: Trust was lower among respondents struggling on present income: 37% among those struggling and 42% among those really struggling said most people can be trusted, compared with 53% overall

social_trust_cost_route.value: Economic insecurity and social trust are patterned together, without a causal direction established

observations.method: Scottish Social Attitudes Survey 2025 core module, with stratified random-probability sampling of Scottish private households and weighted analysis; fieldwork used web and alternative telephone modes.
observations.uncertainty: The income-trust comparison is descriptive and cross-sectional; it does not establish whether economic insecurity reduces trust, low trust affects economic outcomes, or both reflect other conditions.
observations.subgroup: Scottish adults, with comparisons by income difficulty and other demographic, economic, and political factors available in supplementary tables.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower trust among financially strained respondents may reflect institutional or neighbourhood exposure, health, age, or selection into hardship rather than a direct income effect.

observations.period: September-November 2025 fieldwork; institutional trust and listening

denominator.unit: completed Scottish Social Attitudes Survey core-module surveys; weighted estimates

trust_scottish_government_best_interest.unit: percent trusting the Scottish Government to work in Scotland's best interests

trust_uk_government_best_interest.unit: percent trusting the UK Government to act in Scotland's best long-term interest

fair_decision_scottish_government.unit: percent trusting the Scottish Government to make fair decisions for different groups

fair_decision_local_council.unit: percent trusting local councils to make fair decisions for different groups

government_listening_scottish.unit: percent saying the Scottish Government is good at listening before decisions

government_listening_uk.unit: percent saying the UK Government is good at listening before decisions

government_listening_local.unit: percent saying local councils are good at listening before decisions

legitimacy_gap.value: Institutional proximity does not remove legitimacy strain: local and Scottish institutions score above UK institutions on trust/listening, but fair-treatment confidence remains low

observations.method: Weighted national survey estimates with time-series comparisons and institution-level contrasts.
observations.uncertainty: Trust and listening are perceptions, not audits of decision quality or actual participation; the publication does not identify which policies or encounters drive the institution differences.
observations.subgroup: Scottish adults evaluating Scottish Government, UK Government, Scottish Parliament, and local councils.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower trust in UK institutions may reflect constitutional preference or responsibility attribution rather than a general proximity effect; local scores may vary sharply across councils.

observations.period: September-November 2025 fieldwork; issue expression and political engagement

denominator.unit: completed Scottish Social Attitudes Survey core-module surveys; weighted estimates

signed_petition.unit: percent reporting signing a petition in recent years to register what they thought about an issue

contacted_local_council.unit: percent reporting contacting their local council

contacted_mp_or_msp.unit: percent reporting contacting an MP or MSP

public_meeting.unit: percent reporting attending a public meeting

no_listed_activity.unit: percent reporting none of the listed political-expression activities

channel_gradient.value: Low-friction or individually addressable channels are more common than collective or institutionally intensive participation

observations.method: Survey checklist of 16 political-expression activities, capturing self-reported participation over the last few years.
observations.uncertainty: The checklist does not measure frequency, effort, success, response, collective efficacy, or whether nonparticipation reflects satisfaction, exclusion, time constraints, or distrust.
observations.subgroup: Scottish adults using petitions, councils, MPs/MSPs, consultations, campaigns, protests, organizations, and public meetings.
observations.counterinterpretation: Petition signing can be an important collective political act rather than merely low-friction participation; activity rankings do not establish a hierarchy of democratic value.

observations.period: September-November 2025 fieldwork; perceived influence, priorities, and durable voting norms

denominator.unit: completed Scottish Social Attitudes Survey core-module surveys; weighted estimates

low_perceived_say.unit: percent scoring 0-4 of 10 on whether Scotland's political system allows people like them to have a say

high_perceived_say.unit: percent scoring 6-10 of 10 on whether the system allows people like them to have a say

citizen_engagement_driver.unit: percent selecting government engagement with citizens as one of the three greatest drivers of trust in the Scottish Government

voting_scottish_parliament.unit: percent saying it is important to vote in Scottish Parliament elections

voting_uk_parliament.unit: percent saying it is important to vote in UK Parliament elections

voting_local.unit: percent saying it is important to vote in local government elections

legitimacy_tension.value: Voting remains normatively important while many respondents feel they have limited influence over government

observations.method: Weighted survey measures of perceived political voice, trust drivers, and the importance of voting.
observations.uncertainty: Importance of voting is not turnout; perceived influence is not actual policy responsiveness; the report does not establish whether participation closes the legitimacy gap.
observations.subgroup: Scottish adults with differing political, economic, educational, and constitutional views.
observations.counterinterpretation: High voting norms can be a source of democratic resilience rather than evidence of legitimacy failure; people may value elections while distrusting particular governments or decision processes.

related_sources.claim: Scottish Social Attitudes Survey collection, methods, and historic comparability context.
Supporting documents, subgroup tables, time-series tables, and technical materials.

boundary: This record adds a Scotland-specific legitimacy route connecting economic insecurity, social trust, institutional fairness/listening, political-expression channels, perceived influence, and durable voting norms. It is a representative survey of attitudes, not an audit of government performance, a causal model of trust, a turnout estimate, or proof that participation changes policy.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Scottish Government publication page and PDF reviewed for sample, fieldwork, trust, fairness, listening, participation, influence, voting, subgroup, and methodological caveat claims.
